newsitem.title: USA: Link seen between job leavers and U.S. inflation.
newsitem.headline: Link seen between job leavers and U.S. inflation.

text.p: Statistics on the willingness of Americans to leave their jobs voluntarily may be an indicator of future inflation, according to a study released Thursday by a Congressional committee.

"Since the 1970s, the share of voluntary job leavers among the unemployed has had a fairly consistent relationship with the inflation rate," the report issued by the Senate Joint Economic Committe said.
The study was prepared by Robert Stein, senior economist for Sen. Connie Mack, the Florida Republican who is vice chairman of the Joint Economic Committee.

"The steadiness of these two statistics over the past few years is not a coincidence," the study said. "If inflation is going to surge it would most likely be preceded by an upswing in voluntary job leavers one year before."

The report suggests that the unusually low levels of job leavers in the current economic explansion may have reduced the risk of a recession, since the Federal Reserve has not needed to raise interest rates to stamp out inflation.
The report cautioned, however, that if a rise in the voluntary job leavers in January turns out to be a trend, the interest-rate picture could change.

"If the next few months sustain this upward trend, we could get a future uptick in the inflation rate, which in turn may result in Fed action that -- although needed for long-term growth -- could slow or even end the current economic expansion."
The number of job leavers as a percent of unemployed civilians jumped in January to 12.3 percent from 11.7 percent in December.
That increase was highlighted by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday in the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress.
He cited the increase as a possible sign that workers may be becoming more confident in the job market after a period in which many felt insecure despite plentiful jobs.
Greater confidence among workers would tend to make them more likely to ask for wage increases and may in part explain why wage gains have picked up lately, the Fed Chairman suggested.
However, he added that as of yet, "the pickup in wage gains has not shown through to underlying price inflation."
